note: Runs from the rural gaiteiros (Codé di Dona, Bitori, Tchota Suari, Fefé di Calbicera) through Bulimundo's and Os Tubarões' electric funaná of 1978-1984 and Finaçon and Kino Cabral's synth funaná of 1987-1992, to the gaita revival of Ferro Gaita from 1997 and one modern pop take (Dino d'Santiago). Bitori's 1998 album with Chando Graciosa was reissued by Analog Africa in 2016 as Legend of Funaná; four tracks come from Ostinato's 1990s compilation Pour Me a Grog, whose original release years are not given.

size.basis: A judgement, not a count; no source counts funaná recordings. What was read: Wikipedia (pt, en) on the 1980s spread through Bulimundo's six albums of 1980-1984, the 1990s internationalisation through Finaçon and the late-1990s return to the gaita with Ferro Gaita; Ostinato Records' note that Ferro Gaita's first album of 1997 sold 40,000 copies; the iTunes Portugal store, which lists a dozen Ferro Gaita albums and singles, ten Kino Cabral albums from 1992 on, and a long run of label compilations (Funaná Hits, Projecto Funaná, Funaná & Batuko, O Midjor di Funáná, 15 Anos de Funaná / Kizomba with 29 tracks) plus a steady flow of new funaná singles 2017-2026. Most traditional gaiteiros (Codé di Dona, Bitori, Tchota Suari) left only one to three albums each. An insider's essential list is about 50 recordings: Bulimundo, Os Tubarões' funanás, Finaçon, Codé di Dona, Zeca and Zezé di Nha Reinalda, Bitori, Tchota Suari, Ferro Gaita and the 1990s gaita revival.
